item.title: Human attention is the new old bottleneck. We have to design for it even more.
item.description: A wide office floor where one person reads at a desk while dozens of screens around them keep filling with new work for them to address.Agents at Anthropic now log six hours for every human hour, and reading their output would eat half a week. The job is to create judgement systems for what deserves attention.On October 16, four researchers at Anthropic published How employment is changing at Anthropic, a study of how its own agents changed the work.Anthropic is one of the companies at the front of this shift, running its own work on the models it builds, so the study is an early read on where other companies are heading.And honestly, it looks like previous studies in new clothing as I have linked below, just accelerated. Read on.Agents work more than humans. Not a surprise.Here are the early results: By August 2026, agents directed by employees were logging six hours for every hour their people worked.Agent sessions spent about 80% of their time idle, waiting for a person to answer. Even for employees who don’t write code, reading everything their agents produced would take more than half the workweek.That’s the reading tax, and every team with agents will pay it.None of this is new — we have decades of research and many, many principles like Automation Bias that we can apply to solve these problems. Now it’s up to us to apply them.This productivity is changing for everyone.Underneath the numbers, the nature of work is changing yet again, and this time it’s turning everyone into a manager instead of a maker of widgets. That makes this a story about human in the loop and who keeps the agency. A person who can’t read what an agent did is still in the loop on paper, while the agent makes the calls.That puts the problem on ground designers, product managers, and researchers already work.Here are seven steps for keeping people in charge of that loop.Measure Reading TimeHerbert Simon saw this coming in 1971. In Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, he wrote that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” with most of the cost landing on whoever receives it. He meant data banks, and the line fits agents better.Gloria Mark at UC Irvine has measured how thin it already is.Her studies from 2016 to 2020 found people stayed on one screen for 47 seconds on average. Her first study, published in 2004, found two and a half minutes, according to the University of California’s How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024.Every agent you add is a new sender in an inbox that was already overflowing with more information.Note: Hours estimated by converting output tokens to words, assuming 0.75 words per token and 250 words read per minute. What’s lost in here is that a lot of work goes unreviewed, no human in the loop.Anthropic measured the agent side the way a designer would, converting each session’s output into words read at 250 words a minute.Even non-technical groups crossed half a workweek of reading.Most days I build now, with a coding agent doing much of the work, and my limit is how much I can read and judge. So treat reading time like page load time, a budget a team sets and defends.What’s lost in here is that a lot of work goes unreviewed, no human in the loop. Four hundred and twenty four hours is a lot more than the 168 a week currently has.If one workflow’s weekly agent output, divided by 250, comes to more hours than anyone has, the workflow has a design problem.Rank Agent RequestsOne Anthropic engineer compared managing agents to babysitting. A child who needs a juice box opened and a child with a cut finger both arrive at full volume, and so do the agents.Hospitals learned what that costs.Joint Commission’s 2013 Sentinel Event Alert on medical device alarm safety estimated that 85% to 99% of alarm signals don’t require clinical intervention. Staff stop hearing them which is alarm fatigue in spades. Its database logged 80 alarm-related deaths between January 2009 and June 2012.An agent that flags everything at the same volume has trained its human to ignore it.Hospitals answered with alarm management: priorities, quiet defaults for routine readings, and a named person who responds. Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown at Xerox PARC described the goal in The Coming Age of Calm Technology in 1996, as technology that moves from the periphery of attention to the center and back.Most agent interfaces skip the periphery and drop every request in the center.Make agents justify a severity level for each request, keep the routine ones in the periphery as a digest, and bring only decisions a person must make to the center.At Anthropic, agents mostly post in channels set aside for Claude-human work, which keeps the threads where people talk readable.Design the Review StepReview is where people pay the reading tax, and it’s where a human in the loop either keeps agency or hands it over. At Anthropic, agent-written code was removed or reverted at the same rates as code the same engineers wrote by hand, though the authors caution that agent errors may be harder to spot.Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer ProductivityPerception is the bigger risk. In Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, a 2025 trial, METR found that 16 experienced developers took 19% longer with artificial intelligence tools after expecting to save 24%.If people can’t tell how long review takes, they can’t tell when they’ve stopped doing it.Andrej Karpathy made the same point in Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), his June 2025 keynote for Y Combinator. Models generate and people verify, he said, so the loop between them should run as fast as possible, with the model kept “on the leash.”My Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines covers what happens when that cycle slackens: people approve what the machine proposes and miss what it never flagged.A review screen should show what changed next to what existed, what the agent checked and skipped, and where each claim came from.Put the riskiest change first, and log review time per item so the team can see the tax.Write Decisions DownA manager’s decisions only count if the agents can see them. Agents reason from whatever people leave in the open. One Anthropic employee’s name stayed on a months-old document about company swag, so agents kept sending them requests for T-shirts and mugs long after the job changed hands.Shopify’s chief executive, Tobias Lütke, gave this work its popular name in June 2025. He preferred “context engineering” to prompt engineering and called it the core skill, as Simon Willison recorded in Context engineering.Anthropic’s engineers add, in Effective context engineering for AI agents, that a model’s context is a finite attention budget. Every loop runs on two budgets, the agent’s context and the person’s reading time.The cheapest way to protect a person’s attention is to write the decision down once, where every agent can find it.At Anthropic, written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred to 8,500 in a year. Meeting time grew 20% for the median employee and agents see none of a meeting unless someone writes it up.For design and research teams, this is familiar work. Decision logs, research repositories, and design rationale used to be documentation few people opened.Now agents read every page, which raises the bar for keeping it current and owned.Manage the AgentsAt Anthropic, a fifth of employees surveyed in April 2026 said their role had shifted from doing the work to managing Claudes, and interviewees described individual contributors making VP-level decisions. Peter Drucker saw the first version of this in The Effective Executive in 1967, writing that “every knowledge worker in a modern organization is an ‘executive’” if they’re responsible for a contribution.Agents extend that to anyone with a login, and Microsoft’s The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born has a name for the role: agent boss.I call it the work about the work, and the report calls the supporting work meta-work: specifications for multi-agent runs, loops where one agent reviews another, and pipeline dashboards.It grew from 10% of employees’ interactive sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Ethan Mollick argues in Management as AI superpower that this is ordinary management. What’s scarce, he writes, is “knowing what to ask for.”Every one of those homemade dashboards is a product nobody designed.Christopher Noessel argued for designing this layer in Designing Agentive Technology in 2017. Anthropic’s content team shows where it leads: the writers behind the greetings on Claude.ai taught agents to write that copy, then moved into writing prompts and evaluations.Designers and researchers already have a manager’s skills here; the job is to claim this layer before it hardens into internal scripts.Hire for JudgmentAt Anthropic, an automated review of interview scorecards found that mentions of candidates’ creative use of artificial intelligence tools roughly tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical ones between 2024 and 2026. For technical candidates, comments on autonomy and judgment rose the most, while domain expertise shrank as a share of the assessment. In effect, Anthropic is hiring managers of agents.Kent Beck, who created extreme programming, saw the split early. In April 2023 he wrote 90% of My Skills Are Now Worth $0, with a subtitle saying the other 10% were worth 1,000 times more.A portfolio of polished screens shows what a model can now produce, and a record of what you rejected shows judgment.The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 found that seven in 10 employers consider analytical thinking a core skill, the top of its list. For anyone in design, research, or product, that changes what goes in a portfolio and what happens in an interview.Show the decision trail: what the agent proposed, what you cut, and why the result held up with users.In interviews, hand candidates a page of agent output with three planted problems, and watch which ones they catch first.Rebuild Entry-Level RolesThe hardest number in the report concerns people never hired. Junior employees’ share of Anthropic’s technical departments slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9%.Anthropic isn’t alone.This is a warning sign.In Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Erik Brynjolfsson and two Stanford colleagues found a 13% relative decline in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations. Not every executive agrees.The Register’s AWS CEO says using AI to replace junior staff is ‘Dumbest thing I’ve ever heard’ covered Matt Garman’s argument from August 2025. Juniors cost the least and use the tools the most, he said, and without them nobody will have learned anything in 10 years.The skill to supervise an agent comes from years of doing the work it now does.Lisanne Bainbridge warned of this in Ironies of Automation in 1983: automate most of a job, and people keep its hardest part, the monitoring, without the practice that built their judgment. Entry-level roles in design and research can be rebuilt around review, with a junior making the first call on agent output and a senior explaining every override.That’s an apprenticeship, and it costs less than hiring a senior who never had one.ConclusionIn 1950, the United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract that Fortune magazine called the Treaty of Detroit. Walter Reuther’s union gave management room to run the plants, and workers got cost-of-living raises, an annual wage increase, pensions, and health benefits.The report reaches for that same settlement and names Anthropic’s version of it on three points:Broad stock ownershipAn early warning system for jobs at riskA priority on moving people into new roles inside the companyMost of us don’t set compensation policy. We do set what agents show people, when they interrupt, and how review works. Those choices decide whether everyone’s new job as a manager comes with real agency or just a sign-off button.Right now whoever builds the dashboard is making them, and designers, researchers, and product managers should be.The study’s framing is careful. Anthropic is one unusual company, growing fast and building the models it uses, so its practices won’t transfer cleanly to anyone else. The direction is still clear enough to act on this quarter. Output keeps getting cheaper while human attention stays fixed, and the people who decide how it gets spent will shape what these teams become.Action itemsMeasure one workflow. Count the words its agents hand a person in a week, divide by 250, and compare the hours with what anyone has.Tier agent requests. Give every request a severity the agent must justify, batch the routine ones into a daily digest, and keep interruptions for decisions only a person can make.Log decisions publicly. After any meeting that changes direction, post the decision and its owner where agents and colleagues both read.Pair juniors on review. Let a junior make the first call on agent output, with a senior explaining every override.ResourcesWilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff, and McCrory, How employment is changing at Anthropic, Anthropic, 2026Herbert Simon, Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, 1971University of California, How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024 (Gloria Mark’s research)The Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals, 2013Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown, The Coming Age of Calm Technology, Xerox PARC, 1996METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, 2025Andrej Karpathy, Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), Y Combinator, 2025Patrick Neeman, Automation Bias, UX GuidelinesSimon Willison, Context engineering, 2025 (quoting Tobias Lütke)Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025Peter Drucker, The Effective Executive, 1967 (quoted from a Fast Company excerpt)Microsoft, The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born, 2025Ethan Mollick, Management as AI superpower, One Useful Thing, 2026Christopher Noessel, Designing Agentive Technology, Rosenfeld Media, 2017Kent Beck, 90% of My Skills Are Now Worth $0, 2023World Economic Forum, The Future of Jobs Report 2025, 2025Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? item.title: Why design (still) matters, Taste is not a methodology, Borrowed slopes
item.description: Weekly curated resources for designers — thinkers and makers.AI companies have spent the past year hiring forward-deployed engineers: engineers who sit inside a customer’s team, hear the problem firsthand, and ship against it. One count of 1,000 listings found the role grew 1,165% in a single year. This year I did a version of that job for my own newsroom, without the title, and it changed how I think about listening.Being heard runs on two clocks. Listening should be slow. Response should be fast.Nobody feels heard by a report →Editor picksBorrowed slopes →When newsrooms reach for the oldest kit in digital design.By Wira Indra KusumaWhat I told the CFO when he asked why design matters →How to show the impact of design outcomes.By Arin BhowmickDesigning for an idea before it exists →On the useful parts that don’t quite fit.By Hiroshi Sato / 佐藤 仁The UX Collective is an independent design publication that elevates unheard design voices and helps designers think more critically about their work.On M.F. Husain and the meanings of orange →Make me thinkWorth building →“Before, a project like this needed justifying. I’d have asked whether I’d use it enough to make the time worthwhile. If I expected to spend weeks on it, I’d have started thinking about other users, pricing, how it could pay for itself.”Design owns coherence →“Established functions are defined not only by their activities, but also the decision rights they own to something that the business considers important. Finance owns capital allocation. Legal owns risk. Marketing owns demand. Sales owns revenue. Engineering owns reliability. What UX/Design typically owns feels like small potatoes — consistency, usability, accessibility. None of which addresses meaningful business value at scale.”Grieving the loss of details →“Before the term “vibecoding” was coined and the industry shifted to valuing programmers primarily for designing architecture, I proudly called myself a coder as opposed to an engineer. In my eyes, this highlighted the way I focused on the details, performance optimization, knowing the intricacies of the language, and being able to explain how things work, as opposed to juggling Java-esque abstractions.”Cool findsEnergy icons: a free, open-source library →Prompt motion: videos made with Claude Opus 5.5 →The convergence of design →Careers & moreGetting good at your job can stop you getting better →Many experienced people plateau out of sight.By Dora CzernaThe AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart →Our ways of working haven’t caught up.By Kate Agena, PhDTaste is not a design methodology →Our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness.By Patrick NeemanSupport the newsletterIf you find our content helpful, here’s how you can support us:Check out this week’s sponsor and support their work tooForward this email to a friend and invite them to subscribeSponsor an editionWhy design (still) matters, Taste is not a methodology, Borrowed slopes was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: What if AI sets us free?
item.description: What can destroy us can also save us. Here’s how I think we can stay in charge of the choice.From the Rocky Horror Picture Show, sourceCasey Harrell is a climate activist. For years, ALS had been slowly taking his speech, until even the people closest to him struggled to understand what he was saying.In July 2023, surgeons at UC Davis implanted tiny sensor arrays in the part of his brain that controls speech. AI learned to read the signals his brain sends when he tries to talk, turned them into words, and spoke those words aloud in a voice rebuilt from old recordings of him.The first time he heard it, he said: “It feels a lot like me.” People who hadn’t heard his voice in a long time cried.I’ve always believed that what can destroy us may also save us. Power can be wielded in many directions. It’s never just black and white.Right now, most people who aren’t tech bros or tech sisses are either avoiding AI altogether or working from a narrow view of what’s actually happening (and what’s possible). Many are scared. The consensus seems to be: AI is coming for us, and that’s probably gonna make everything worse.After a global pandemic and a fresh round of nuclear anxiety, AI feels like the next unprecedented thing. The one that might finally be the nail in humanity’s coffin.But what if it’s not?‘Good’ AI is a choice.What intrigues me about AI is exactly this power: the potential for harm is enormous, which means the potential for good is too. Yin and yang.So what if it all goes right?Humans have always been driven by what if. It’s how we’ve crossed oceans, tamed fire, and ended up, well, here.Exactly here. Collective anxiety, crisis, tech that seems to be racing away from us. It’s no coincidence.But that potential. The opportunity. The blank canvas. The thrill of not knowing exactly what will come out of something is as scary as it is fascinating. And it’s what we’ve always been pushing towards.This exciting sweet spot between what’s possible now and what it might make possible is what got me into designing products for a living.And if that work has taught me one thing, it’s that technology is never neutral. Every product is a stack of decisions: who it serves, what it rewards, what it refuses to do. A feed that keeps you scrolling at 2 am is a design choice. So is a tool that hands you back your evening.And the good AI stories, while harder to find in an endless feed of doom and gloom, are not lucky accidents. In every one of them, someone decided who it was for, put the right people in the room, and kept humans in charge.Good is a choice someone made. What if we make more of those?Yes.What if?What if it cures cancer?AI is already catching cancer earlier.Here in Sweden, Lund University ran the MASAI trial. Around 106,000 women in the Swedish screening programme were split in two: half had their mammograms read the traditional way, half with AI support. The AI group saw 29% more cancers detected. The final results showed 12% fewer cancers slipping through between screenings. Fewer of the aggressive kind, too.As a carrier of the breast cancer gene, with at least one mammogram a year since I turned 30, I’ve spent nights worrying, not about my own risk, but about my daughters’. What if AI solves breast cancer?Zoom out from one disease to all of biology. For 50 years, working out the 3D shape of a single protein could take a scientist years. In 2020, DeepMind’s AlphaFold learned to predict those shapes from a sequence alone. Two years later, its team released predicted structures for more than 200 million proteins. It has since been used by over three million researchers in more than 190 countries. The creators have won the Nobel Prize.And then there are the superbugs. At MIT, researchers trained an AI to scan more than 100 million chemical compounds for ones that could kill bacteria. It found halicin, which killed strains resistant to every known antibiotic in lab tests, and later abaucin. Halicin is named after HAL, the murderous computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey. A reference to its significance.The machine we were taught to fear is finding essential medicine.What if interfaces fit every body and every mind?For all of computing history, people have had to adapt to the machine.AI is starting to flip that. Now.Be My Eyes started in Denmark, founded by a blind furniture craftsman, as an app connecting blind people with sighted volunteers over video. In 2023, it added Be My AI: point your phone at a menu, a medicine label, or your outfit, and get a detailed description back.Casey Harrell, whose story opened this piece, is the far end of the same idea: an interface that adapts so completely it meets you inside your own body — and maybe even mind.So while most AI applications may feel like a boost for mass production, the opposite is also true. For the first time ever, we can create interfaces that shape themselves to us. Our eyes, our voices, our attention spans, our bad days. We can finally kill the norm and build custom at scale.What if it gives artists better access to tools?A friend told me about how low-income filmmakers in his community can now tell their stories due to accessible generative AI for film. And while “made without AI” is more meaningful, showcasing their storytelling skills may be the way to access funding that was limited to privileged groups.I also see this in my life. It’s now easier for me to reformat my writing to make it easier to distribute, type off my handwriting to an online doc, and automate the organization layer of my creative process to allow me more time to actually create.Last month I built an entire app to help me keep track of my ideas as voice notes. It auto-categorizes them and surfaces them back to me based on what I’m doing and where I am. It’s been a game changer for my process and one of the most fun things I’ve done lately: the app’s design is inspired by my kids’ squishy obsession, so the visuals and haptics are satisfying to watch, and tinkering with them was as fun as working on my usual pottery.What if AI gives back to Earth?Rainforest Connection hangs solar-powered listening devices in the canopy. AI listens for chainsaws, trucks and gunshots, and pings rangers’ phones the moment it hears one. The rangers from the Indigenous Tembé community use it to defend their land. The network now covers more than 736,000 hectares in 37 countries. What if we can protect the Earth before it’s too late?Floods affect around 250 million people a year. Google’s Flood Hub uses AI to forecast river floods up to seven days ahead, even where there are no river gauges, and now covers places where 700 million people live, in over 100 countries. Google says flood forecasting in Africa is now on par with Europe. I can imagine there’s even more tech that can do to protect us.There’s more to planet Earth than nature, so…What if it helps unite us, humans?In 2024, DeepMind researchers built an AI mediator, named the Habermas Machine (after one of my favorite German philosophers), and tested it with more than 5,000 people debating divisive issues. People preferred its summaries to a human mediator’s, groups moved closer together, and it worked minority objections into the final conclusion so everyone felt heard. The team behind it trained Habermas to mediate, not to persuade. The job was to find where people already agreed and write it down. If you think about it, it’s the same kind of technology behind the outrage engine of our feeds, just pointed the other way.Could something like this eventually bring us closer together? Make us comfortable discussing and disagreeing again, so we can move toward a compromise and away from extremes and isolation?AI as a peacekeeper. A tempting thought. A machine that helps us hear each other might be a step in the right direction.What if it doesn’t take our jobs?For most, this is the scariest part.And yes, jobs will disappear. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025, based on more than 1,000 employers, expects 92 million jobs to be displaced by 2030 and 170 million new ones created, a net gain of 78 million. The fastest growth is expected in frontline human work like care and education.Forecasts are guesses, though. And even if you believe this optimistic prediction, a net gain is no comfort if the job lost is yours — or if your next one might only be available after years of retraining.I think the truth is somewhere in the middle.In 2024, Klarna announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 customer service agents and handling two-thirds of its customer chats. About a year later, its CEO said the quality had suffered, and the company started hiring humans again.What I’m trying to get at is this:AI built to replace people tends to make things worse. AI built to support people tends to make things better.MASAI didn’t fire radiologists; it gave them back 44% of their reading time. Casey Harrell didn’t need a new voice; he needed his own.Whether AI takes our jobs or transforms them isn’t decided by the technology. It’s decided by people in meeting rooms, choosing what to automate and what to protect. Some of those people are designers. I’m one of them.Most of those people do care.I choose to believe that they, like me, take their responsibility personally and seriously. And that we can and will figure out a way to make AI work for good.What if it actually frees up our time?Last week, my friends over at Sanna, a Norwegian AI-accounting startup, announced that they were introducing a 4-day work week for their accountants.In 2019, Finland’s then-future prime minister asked on a party panel why a four-day week or a six-hour day couldn’t be the next step, and whether eight hours was really the ultimate truth. It never became Finnish policy, but the question stuck. And we now know the answer can be yes. In the UK’s 2022 pilot, 61 companies cut hours with no cut in pay. Revenue held steady, resignations fell by 57%, and 56 of the 61 kept the shorter week.I am hopeful that AI will finally be the technology that doesn’t turn efficiency into more work — because now the gains are so obvious, why would we not spend them on leisure, self-fulfillment, being with each other? Not doing that feels insane to me. I’m sure I’m not the only one.I can imagine it.A Friday that belongs to me: reading, writing, hanging with my kids, or maybe doing nothing at all. The stuff of Renaissance paintings. And maybe our future?From The Laziest People in Art, sourceWhat if it takes us offline?This is my most hopeful what if.Almost every example in this piece still happens on a screen. That’s where we are. Right now. But I don’t think it’s where we’re headed. Screens add a digital layer to life that takes away from our lived experience.I’ve always thought screens were never the point. I’m almost sure you’d agree.We stare at our phones because that’s where the doing happens: the booking, the paying, the replying, the finding. Endless apps, each built to keep us locked in. If AI can do the doing, the reason to stare goes away. You say what you need, and get on with your day. And even further: what if you don’t have to be proactive at all; it can organize based on what it learns about you. The interface becomes secondary. Maybe, it goes away.Think back to Be My AI. A blind user points a phone at a menu, hears what’s on it, and puts the phone back in her pocket. Think of Casey Harrell, speaking with no screen at all. The most advanced interfaces are already the ones that disappear.Wouldn’t it be funny if AI is what finally breaks our phone addictions?And there’s another argument.When content becomes infinite and basically free, it stops being worth much. One-to-infinite, the logic of the feed, gets flooded with sameness. And when everything is generic, what becomes valuable again is the specific: the handmade, the local, the person who actually knows you, the things you can touch. With your heart, mind, and soul.One-to-one, not one-to-infinite (I wrote about this before, here).What if AI pushes our tech obsession so far that it solves it? It runs itself in the background. And we just do us.Humans, human to human, together.Don’t dream it, be it.None of my musings cancel the risks. AI can (and already is) be(ing) used to surveil, manipulate, replace, and harm, and people far more qualified than me are right to sound the alarm.But — I hope this came across in my piece — there is as much potential for good as for evil. Yin and Yang.The future isn’t something that happens to us.It’s something we build. And we can only build toward what we can imagine. If the only story we tell about AI is the one where it ends us, we leave the steering wheel to the people who don’t mind that ending. It’s their greatest weapon: to make us feel defeated, choiceless, numb.From the Rocky Horror Picture show, sourceSo this is for the people who make things.The designers, the writers, the engineers, the product people, the ones in the meeting rooms. We are the ones deciding, one screen, one button, one sentence at a time, what this technology rewards and what it refuses to do.Ask who it’s for.Put the right people in the room.Keep humans in charge. MASAI kept a radiologist in the loop; Rainforest Connection put the tool in the hands of the Tembé rangers rather than a central authority.Let’s build the version you’d want your mother to use at 3 am or your daughter to carry in 20 years.And for everyone else: stay curious. Look past the headlines. Ask for the good version. Demand it. Stray from your feed. Occasionally, turn off the news.Who knows what will happen? What can destroy us may also save us. Believing it might save us is our only chance.So: what if it all goes right?What if, one day, we look at the world we built with it, and say what Casey Harrell said when he heard himself again?It feels a lot like us.Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.What if AI sets us free? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: UX designers are not designing interfaces, they design personalities
item.description: How tech culture impacts how we understand ourselves through appsPhoto by blue sky on UnsplashIn the last 20 years, the tech world has transformed parts of humanity into one-dimensional digital zombies. Sadly, you can hold me personally responsible. Let me tell you why. It started in 1995, when I was 12 years old, and our household got access to the web. An internet connection was needed because my parents had an advertising agency located in an office next to our house. The World Wide Web allowed my folks to send documents to print shops without having to drive there in person.My parents’ agency did things like branding, marketing campaigns, and product packaging designs. In the mid ’90s, my parents’ clients understood that the internet was ‘the next big thing.’ They said that ‘they had to do something with the internet.’ In other words, they wanted a website. There was no real strategy behind the need to have a website. Online presence was a goal in itself. And I could help them fulfil this goal.As a nerdy teenager, I taught myself to write HTML and design interfaces. With my newly acquired skills, I was able to build websites for my parents’ customers. In reality, these companies would give me one of their paper brochures and tell me to ‘make this a website.’ The very first corporate websites were just elaborate business cards: a description, a photo, a list of their services, and contact details.One of the first “masterpieces” I designed in the ’90sThe interactive webMy teenage years in the ’90s, and my role as (what was then called) a webmaster, gave me much satisfaction. Over the following years, the web changed. Websites became more interactive. Webshops and social media emerged. Users could now also actively participate. They could add content and communicate with one another.Perhaps the first interactive system I designed was a portal that enabled companies to offer health services to their staff. Through this platform, workers could get free gym memberships. Of course, on the platform, staff members could monitor their health progress. More significantly, their bosses could also scrutinise the overall fitness of their workforce. The platform enabled the company to measure the relationship between HR investments and sick leave. Where does the sweet spot lie between paying for health services and reduced costs related to staff absences? At the time, I thought I was designing a health platform, but what I was really designing was workforce optimisation.The heath app I designedWeb Design to User ExperienceOver time, my job title changed from Web Designer to User Experience Designer. I got an updated, fancier title that looks cool on a business card or LinkedIn. My role suggested I wasn’t just designing websites anymore. Somehow, I was designing experiences. I was crafting how people interact with a digital product and how they interpret the interfaces and information they are exposed to.In other words, I was designing comprehension and behaviour. Or… was I producing something even more fundamental? Was I perhaps designing how people see themselves? Or even more elemental, was I nudging people into becoming someone different?As the technical possibilities of the web advanced, my work became more and more concerned with what happened after a website was launched. The website itself wasn’t about the finished product. The industry began tracking what people did with it. Tools such as Google Analytics allowed companies to see how far people scrolled, how long they stayed on a page, and which actions they completed. Suddenly, the behaviour of website users could be analysed in detail.My job shifted from making websites look and feel nice, or, as I would say at the time, cool, to optimising how people interacted with them. The importance of aesthetics was being overtaken by concepts like conversion optimisation.The role of the metricAt the level of the tech worker, my own productivity started to be monitored. This was done through corporate frameworks like Agile and software, especially Atlassian products. I delivered story points and maintained velocity instead of just (giving my boss the illusion I was) working hard. All of a sudden, I was dealing with standups, tickets, and dashboards.Because a website wasn’t seen as a finished product anymore, features could be added or optimised at any time, based on new insights from metrics. Time-boxed projects became ongoing trajectories without a specific end. Clients wouldn’t pay for a finished website, but would purchase an ‘envelope of time’ designers and engineers could spend on ongoing improvements. Project management turned into product management. This way, teams could quickly respond to changing requirements. Teams became agile.Measuring the website became part of a larger move in which success was defined by performance metrics. In addition to being measured myself through story points and velocity, this calculative logic moved into the product. The metrics that guided companies became metrics inside apps. The metrics that governed workers transitioned into metrics that influenced users.A website became something that could be continuously measured, tested and improved. This seemed totally sensible. Why wouldn’t we want to know whether our designs worked and how we could improve? These are valid questions. However, there is a downside to measuring. It defines what counts as knowledge. What can be measured becomes a particular form of authority. The things captured in Google Analytics become more important than aspects of the user that can’t be metrified.Companies use (Agile) frameworks to measure workers. Workers build products that measure users. Users then measure themselves (and each other).The blind spot of the metricWhen I entered the tech industry, the web was still relatively young. Websites became platforms, projects turned into products, and analytics were embedded in decision-making. Measurement moved from being something that was ‘interesting’ and was used occasionally to a form of knowledge that structured every aspect of my work. Metrics became what we would see as ‘true’.A metric tells something about reality. More significantly, it selects what part of reality becomes visible. Not only for the company and tech teams, but also for the users. Other things may still exist. Yet, they become harder to see. The number of story points you deliver shows something about your contribution, but it doesn’t take into account the support you gave your colleague or the time you spent on the phone with a client. For the user, a 10,000-step achievement might indicate a healthy person, but the metric doesn’t show what the person drank or ate that day.Fitbit tracking — SourceAgile, product, and user metrics allow for classifying employees and products. User-targeted metrics do that too. They make it possible to categorise, rank, and compare users. An Uber rating helps the platform assess passengers and drivers. One user with a rating of 4.86 doesn’t mean much, but when millions of users are rated, it gives a lot of information. Metrics turn complex human beings into comparable profiles and enable platforms to make decisions.Body or codeLet’s look at the user a bit more in detail to illustrate how metrics affect them. What happens when metrics become the primary way through which users understand themselves? In that case, the metric begins to compete with our real lived experience. I discovered this personally when I started using Fitbit. I had been having problems with my sleep, and I thought a health app could help me understand what on earth was going on. At first, I wanted to see on which days my sleep was worse. What was the cause of these bad nights? Maybe Fitbit could help me.The old me would wake up and simply decide how I felt. If I had slept badly, I might take it easy in the morning. If I felt rested, I would probably do an early morning workout. My experience of my own body was the primary source of information. There was no score telling me whether I had slept well or badly.The Fitbit-me looked at my app the moment I woke up. My night was translated into data. Sleep duration, time to fall asleep, deep sleep, REM sleep, and all that jazz are displayed on a screen. I might be told that I slept for 6 hours 39 minutes and that my sleep score was 68. Fitbit could tell me that I had less deep sleep than usual, or that my sleep was below my personal average.When Fitbit would tell me I had a few nights of poor sleep, I would start to get nervous. I knew ‘for a fact’ I needed a good night’s sleep because I had a few bad ones. I considered Fitbit a more reliable source of information than my own perception. The metric became my reality. Obviously, going to bed feeling stressed will not lead to better sleep. I would go to bed early but lie awake for a long time.Fitbit’s sleep dashboards (2019)Finding truth in a health wearable is different from being rated as an Uber driver or having work tracked in Jira. Although all three forms of knowledge rely on metrics, the metrics influence how we understand ourselves differently.When I look at my Fitbit score, I might doubt my own bodily experience. I can wake up feeling rested, but if the app tells me that I had a bad night. I might consider the score more reliable than my own feeling. The metric changes how I interpret myself.For a taxi driver, the Uber rating reflects how other people evaluate them. A driver may therefore adjust their behaviour to avoid a poor rating. The metric creates an incentive to behave in a certain way.In Jira, story points and velocity make work visible within an organisation. Yet, they cannot capture everything that makes someone a valuable colleague. Helping a struggling teammate may contribute to a team’s success but is not included in story points. This way, workers may prioritise what counts as measurable output over what matters in the work itself.The way the metric functions is thus different, depending on the context. What connects these examples is that each makes a particular aspect of life visible. Only a selected part of reality becomes meaningful. Based on this meaning, people change their behaviour. They change how they sleep, drive, or work. They understand their sleep or work through the metric.The homo metricusSo what happens when we allow a metric to determine how we understand ourselves? Let’s go back to our work as UX designers. I have spent most of my professional life designing things that mediate how people understand and act in the world. For a long time, I thought the important question was whether my interfaces were easy to use. Whether they provided a good User Experience.Then I started wondering whether they were doing something more fundamental. Maybe technology doesn’t just change how we do things and what we do. Maybe it also changes how we understand what/who we are.The metrics inside our workplaces, our apps, and our wearables may seem to be nothing more than useful representations of reality. But, once metrics become part of the environments in which we act, they can also become part of how we understand ourselves.This sounds abstract, but it isn’t. Users care about how many people liked their story, what their credit score or Airbnb rating is, or how long their Duolingo streak is. Users accept metrics imposed by the tech platform as part of their daily routine. What do you do when your follower count stagnates, you deliver fewer story points than usual, or see your Uber passenger score fall?Eventually, we may find ourselves living according to metrics that we helped create by contributing data. I call the person produced by this environment the homo metricus.The homo metricus is someone who understands and governs itself through algorithmically defined metrics.Obviously, I didn’t set out to become a homo metricus. No one does. But that doesn’t mean that we aren’t a homo metricus in some way or form. We take some of the metrics that tech platforms (including Atlassian) introduce awfully seriously. (Read more about the homo metricus in this post).Uber drivers are exposed to a lot of tracking — SourceThe role of the designerWhen I entered the tech industry, the web was a collection of pages. In fact, there was even a directory that aimed to list all the websites in the world. Over time, websites became platforms, projects became products, and analytics became embedded in decision-making. Measurement moved from something we used occasionally to a way to structure our work. The metric then travelled from the tech company to the user. Users began measuring themselves and each other.This doesn’t mean that metrics are bad, per se. Metrics can make things visible that would otherwise be hard to see. They can help us understand our behaviour and improve what we do. However, we might occasionally forget that a metric is only a representation of a part of reality. Things not captured by the metric still exist.Be honest with yourself... How intensely do you look at numbers? As a tech worker, how much do you care about your story points, velocity, 360-feedback score, etc. As a designer, how much do you look at churn rate, conversion numbers, and A/B tests? As a user, how much do you look at metrics provided by Uber, Instagram, Fitbit, Duolingo or any other app you use frequently?As UX designers, one thing is to acknowledge how we are governed by (Agile) numbers. We should also be very mindful of the limited reality that metrics create. Everything that is not captured by the metric still exists. Ultimately, we, as UX designers, need to understand how the metrics we add to products change how people behave. We are not designing experiences. We are designing how people understand the world and themselves. We are designing the homo metricus.So how can we design a UX that reduces how much the user relies on metrics without eliminating their benefits? We can’t remove the metric. It’s often a big part of the UX and helps the company to achieve its business objectives.However, we can give the metric less authority. The Fitbit app, for instance, could show the sleep score together with the user’s own self-reported idea of how rested they feel. Jira could acknowledge the value of helping colleagues instead of treating completed story points as the only indication of contribution.In real life, people can take off their wearable because they get tired of always seeing their steps. These options can also be added to the UX itself.As designers, we can search for ways that give the metric more open to interpretation. This less metric-centric UX will leave room for parts of life that can’t be quantified. It may still give the metric authority, but not the only one.This article is ultimately about how business metrics become metrics that are embedded in apps. We, as designers, should analyse where the metrics we introduce come from and what they are intended to achieve. How do they contribute to the performance metrics of our business? Is the metric the only way this objective can be achieved? Or are there alternatives?As UX designers, we might be able to decide which metrics are dominant, and which alternatives could be available. Through our UXs and metrics, we are helping shape how people understand themselves. Let’s not make them fully developed homo metrici. What solutions or adjustments would you propose?This article covers a very limited message of my upcoming book with the working title “Homo Metricus — How smartphone apps change what it means to be human.” In the upcoming period, I will post more insights to explore the relationship between humanity, tech platforms, and metrics.SourcesMy ideas are partially a contemporary bastardisation/reinterpretation of Michel Foucault’s later work. Other philosophical theories that cover related social problems can be found in the writings of Alain Supiot, Gilles Deleuze, and Herbert Marcuse.UX designers are not designing interfaces, they design personalities was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Beyond the Canvas
item.description: What Config India 2026 revealed about the expanding possibilities of design.Something is changing in the world of design, and Bengaluru offered a fascinating glimpse of where it’s heading. Thousands of designers, exciting new capabilities, and conversations that went far beyond the latest Figma features. One message stood out: “Design is the differentiator.” Designers are gaining unprecedented capabilities to turn ideas into working products, while India’s technology leaders are making design central to how they build and compete.Design is entering a new era of influence and designers have an opportunity to shape far more than interfaces. The question is no longer what designers can create, but how much of the future they’re prepared to shape.Figma Config India 2026 — Official event artwork. Bengaluru, 15 October 2026. Source: https://config.figma.com/india/The canvas is no longer the limitFor years, design software has been bringing designers closer to the products they imagine, the distance between an idea and a working experience has been getting shorter. But this evolution is accelerating, with much bigger implications for the role of designers.At Config India, Dylan Field made a compelling argument: as code becomes easier to produce, design is increasingly the differentiator. The latest capabilities make that shift tangible. Designers can explore ideas directly in code, engineers can work on the canvas, and AI agents can participate in the same creative process. The traditional boundaries between design and engineering are becoming increasingly fluid.Designers should take greater ownership of what they create. For too long, we’ve accepted that our responsibility ends at handoff. As the barriers between design and engineering disappear, that boundary makes less and less sense. We don’t all need to become software engineers, but we should be accountable for the experience people actually use, not just the one we designed.Dylan Field, CEO and co-founder of Figma. Config India 2026, Bengaluru.Your next design colleague isn’t humanAI is quickly becoming part of the designer’s everyday toolkit. But the more interesting evolution is happening in how we work with it. Until recently, much of our interaction with AI was transactional: write a prompt, get a result, refine it and repeat. What happens when an AI agent becomes a genuine collaborator, able to understand the context of a project, follow its rules and contribute alongside the rest of the team?The latest Figma announcements bring this vision closer to reality. Code Layers brings running code into Figma’s collaborative canvas, Specs provides shared context for people and agents, and Payload connects content and backend capabilities to the creation process. Together, they open the possibility of AI agents working with the same context, designs and decisions as their human colleagues.“I find the idea of AI as a new colleague more compelling than AI as another productivity tool. But a capable colleague is only as effective as the context, direction and judgement surrounding their work.”Design teams will need to become better at expressing intent, making decisions explicit and creating environments where humans and agents can contribute without losing coherence. The next generation of designers won’t simply be defined by how well they use AI, but by how well they lead the work they do with it.The rise of the design engineerDesigners who code are nothing new. Design engineers have been bridging creativity and technology for years, translating ideas into functioning experiences. What is changing is how essential that expertise is becoming. As AI accelerates development and the boundaries between design and engineering blur, the ability to connect design intent with technical implementation is moving from a specialist advantage to a capability every design organisation needs.Parinishtha Yadav, Principal Design Manager at Microsoft, challenged designers to take ownership of the entire front end, including the build. This thinking is also shared by TJ Pitre, Product Architect for AI & Design Systems at Figma, who sees design systems as “a collection of decisions”, rather than simply libraries of components.If AI agents are going to build with our design systems, they need to understand the thinking and principles behind them, not just the components. Design engineering is becoming indispensable to the modern design organisation. The challenge is no longer simply maintaining consistency across screens, but ensuring that design intent survives the journey from human decisions to machine-generated experiences. This requires people who can think in systems, understand code and translate design principles into rules that technology can follow. The future of design systems won’t be measured by how many components they contain, but by how intelligently those components can be used.Parinishtha Yadav, Principal Design Manager at Microsoft. Config India 2026, Bengaluru.Designing at the speed of thought. But should we?We are entering an era where the distance between an idea and a working product can shrink dramatically. AI can help us explore concepts, generate interfaces and build functioning prototypes in minutes rather than days. The promise of designing at the speed of thought is exciting. But it raises a question I believe every designer should be asking: just because we can move faster, does that mean we should?While Dylan Field demonstrated how AI workflows are accelerating the creative process, some of the most interesting conversations were about knowing when to slow down. Tarun Mehta, co-founder of Ather Energy, described testing unfinished prototypes, sometimes something as simple as a seat, and organising demo days to learn from customers. Nav Pawera, speaking about designing public services, questioned whether we really need to move so fast. They were reminders that building something quickly and understanding whether it should be built are two different things.I believe speed is becoming one of the most overrated measures of design progress. Faster execution is valuable when it gives us more opportunities to experiment, learn and improve. But when speed becomes the objective, we risk accelerating towards solutions we haven’t properly questioned. It’s like being handed a faster car: without knowing where we’re going or how to handle it, we’re simply increasing the chances of a crash.“The best designers won’t be those who move the fastest, but those who know when to accelerate, when to slow down and when to change direction.”Ather Energy’s electric scooter. A reminder of Tarun Mehta’s approach to prototyping, testing and learning from customers. Source: https://www.atherenergy.com/The CEO is part of the design teamFor years, designers have been fighting for a seat at the table, trying to convince executives that design deserves a voice in strategic decisions. But what happens when the executives themselves think like designers? At the Figma Leadership Collective, I was struck by how deeply three of India’s most successful technology founders were involved in the design of their products. They weren’t simply sponsoring design or reviewing the final results. They were getting their hands dirty, questioning interactions, testing ideas and staying remarkably close to their customers.During the panel Beyond the Noise: Building Products People Can’t Ignore, Harshil Mathur of Razorpay, Sri Harsha Majety of Swiggy and Tarun Mehta of Ather Energy shared a remarkably consistent philosophy: build for customers, not for headlines. Harshil questioned whether familiar interfaces such as dashboards would remain relevant as AI agents change how people consume information. Tarun described taking even the simplest prototypes directly to people, organising demo days and learning through constant iteration. What impressed me was how naturally all three founders discussed design, with the curiosity and attention to detail I would expect from experienced designers.“I left that conversation convinced that design literacy is becoming an executive competency.”The most influential product leaders understand how experiences are conceived, tested and refined, because those decisions are inseparable from business strategy. And perhaps that’s the bigger lesson for our profession. We spend so much energy trying to bring design into the boardroom, when we should also be asking how to bring design thinking into the minds of those already sitting there. The real victory for design isn’t earning a seat at the table. It’s becoming part of how everyone at that table thinks.Who are we building the future for?We often measure technological progress by how intelligent, powerful or sophisticated our products become. But perhaps a more meaningful measure is how many people can actually benefit from them. AI offers an extraordinary opportunity to make technology more accessible, to remove barriers of language, knowledge and technical expertise, and to give people capabilities that were previously reserved for specialists. For designers, this opens an exciting possibility: creating experiences that reach and empower people we have never been able to serve effectively before.At the Leadership Collective, Pratyush Kumar, co-founder of Sarvam AI, brought this ambition to life. Sarvam is building AI for India, with local languages and cultural context at its foundation. What stayed with me was his conviction that AI should not become something mythical or inaccessible. People should be able to understand it, experiment with it and create with it themselves. He also spoke about the importance of Indian talent building technology in India, for Indian needs. There was something genuinely optimistic about this vision: technology shaped by the people and communities it is intended to serve.“As designers gain the power to build almost anything, we have a responsibility to ask who benefits from what we create.”I believe the democratisation of intelligence could become one of the most important opportunities in the history of design. But accessibility means more than making a product available or translating an interface. It requires understanding people’s languages, circumstances, abilities and aspirations, and giving them the confidence to participate. As designers gain the power to build almost anything, we have a responsibility to ask who benefits from what we create. The greatest achievement of AI may not be making technology more intelligent, but making its possibilities available to everyone.Visual elements from Sarvam AI. Source: https://www.sarvam.ai/What a time to be a designerI came to Bengaluru for design, but India gave me much more to think about. The city is fascinating, full of contrasts and extraordinary energy. What struck me most was the ambition of its creative community. Thousands of designers coming together, founders who speak the language of design, and a generation of talent eager to build what comes next. Throughout the week, I encountered a remarkable combination of creativity, technical confidence, cultural pride and openness. I arrived expecting to discover the latest innovations in design. I left with the feeling that India is already helping define its future.And perhaps Bengaluru was the perfect place to witness this moment in our profession. On one side, AI is giving designers unprecedented capabilities to imagine, prototype and build. On the other, design is becoming increasingly central to how companies innovate, how leaders make decisions and how technology reaches people. What impressed me about India was how naturally these two movements seemed to come together. From founders personally testing prototypes to teams building AI for their own languages and communities, design was being treated as both a creative capability and a strategic responsibility.This is what I take away from Config India. The opportunity ahead of us is extraordinary, but greater capability alone doesn’t guarantee better outcomes. We can build faster, collaborate with intelligent agents and turn ideas into functioning products with less friction than ever before. The real question is what we choose to do with that power. Will we simply produce more, or will we use it to understand people better, challenge assumptions and create things that genuinely matter?The future of design will be defined not only by what designers can create, but by what they are empowered to shape.Further reading and referencesIf you’re curious to explore some of the ideas, conversations and projects mentioned in this article, here are a few useful links:Config India 2026 — Official Agenda and Sessions — Figma: https://config.figma.com/india/agenda/Build by Design: New Workflows for New Ways of Building — Dylan Field, Figma’s Config India keynote and product announcements: https://www.figma.com/blog/build-by-design/Design Systems Are a Collection of Decisions — TJ Pitre: https://southleft.substack.com/p/design-systems-are-a-collection-ofFigma Deepens Investment in India — Figma’s announcement, including its partnership with Sarvam AI: https://www.figma.com/blog/figma-deepens-investment-in-india/Ather Energy — Electric mobility, product innovation and design: https://www.atherenergy.com/Beyond the Canvas was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Design in the material you ship
item.description: Designers should understand code the way an architect understands stone: what it can do, not how to cut it. AI now does the cutting.The same card in the design file and in the browser with real data. Image by the author.Early in The Fountainhead, Howard Roark is expelled from architecture school for refusing to design in borrowed styles. The Dean calls him in to explain himself, and Roark gives him a rule instead: “What can be done with one substance must never be done with another. No two materials are alike. No two sites on earth are alike. No two buildings have the same purpose. The purpose, the site, the material determine the shape.”You don’t have to admire Roark to take the point. He is the architect in the book who spends his time on building sites, among the electricians and steelworkers, learning what the material will and won’t do. His classmates learn to draw facades.Digital designers have a material too. It is code. For most of the last fifteen years, we have designed in pictures of it. The warning is older than that. John Allsopp asked the web to stop imitating print in 2000, Frank Chimero wrote about working with the web’s grain in 2015, and Jeremy Keith gave its materials a chapter of their own in Resilient Web Design.The drawing is not the buildingA design file is a drawing. It shows one state, at one width, in one language, with the data the designer typed in. The product is every other state.The name is longer than the box. A short English label can double in length once it is translated. The photo fails to load. The list is empty. The request takes four seconds, or fails. Someone tabs through with a keyboard. The phone is 320 pixels wide. None of those is an edge case to the person it happens to, and none of them exists in the file until someone draws it by hand, which in practice means rarely.Six states the design file never showed. Image by the author.When the file is the source of truth, each of those gaps gets decided by whoever writes the code, after the design is called done, and usually without a conversation. The file and the product drift apart, and the file keeps being presented in reviews as if it were the product.What changed when the code became the sourceWhen I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, I built them in code. The surprise was what happened to the specification. In a design file, a jelly button is an adjective: tactile. In code, it is a handful of numbers. The pointer starts to count 36 pixels from the edge, the material has a stiffness, and it settles back in under a second. An engineer can build a number. Nobody can build an adjective.One of 131 button variations, built in code. Image by the author.I now work the same way on a product team. The prototype in code is what gets reviewed. The design file still exists, because people like to leave comments on a canvas, but it is regenerated from the code after each pass, never the other way round. Its job is to be a mirror.Before and after: which artifact is the source of truth. Image by the author.Roark’s rule applies almost word for word. A responsive layout, a loading state and a focus ring belong to the browser. Drawing them in a canvas tool is doing with one substance what belongs to another.You no longer have to write itThis is where the old version of the argument went wrong. For a decade, “designers should code” meant designers should learn to write HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Many tried, many quit, and they were right to resent it. It asked them to become a second, slower engineer. Brad Frost later drew a more useful line, between the front of the front end, which sits close to design, and the application logic behind it.That argument is over, because AI writes the code. I describe the screen, its states and its numbers, and the model writes it. I correct it by looking at the result and saying what is wrong, the way an architect corrects a site, not by laying the bricks again myself.Reading code is going the same way. It still helps, and I read diffs most days. But AI review tools read them too, and they are improving quickly. In one benchmark this year, the best reviewer caught 84 of 122 real bugs taken from production codebases such as Sentry and Grafana. The vendor that won ran the test, and two thirds is not all of them. So the claim is not that the machine has replaced the reviewer. It is that the designer no longer needs to be the reviewer.Who writes, reads and understands the code. Image by the author.Engineers reading this will object, and they have a point. In Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey, 66 percent named AI answers that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration, and 46 percent said they distrust its accuracy. Someone accountable for the system still has to read what goes into it. That person is the engineer who owns it. The designer has a different job.Understanding is the part you can’t delegateWhat Roark took from the building site was not the skill of riveting. It was knowing what steel will do, so that his drawings only asked for things the material could give.That is the part AI can’t hold for you. It will write whatever you describe, including things the medium handles badly, and it will review the code against the code, not against what the person on the other end needed. Judging that takes someone who knows the material.You judge the output by running it, not by reading it. Open it at 320 pixels. Paste the longest real name you can find. Set the network to slow. Put the mouse away and use the keyboard. None of those tests needs a line of syntax.What to learn instead of syntaxHow layout flows: what wraps, what stretches, what refuses to shrink.Which states exist: empty, loading, partial, failed, offline.The shape of the data, including what a field holds when it holds nothing.What costs a trip to the server and what is free on the device.What a screen reader actually announces on your screen.How to run the product on your own machine, without help.How to ask the AI to explain a change in plain words.None of these requires writing code. All of them require spending time with it.The material determines the shapeRoark’s rule ends where this argument does: the purpose, the site and the material determine the shape. Our material hasn’t changed. It is still code, and it still decides what a screen can be. What changed is that we no longer have to hold the chisel to learn what it can cut.Design in the material you ship was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
